Chapter 7: The Myth of Endless Growth
You know, there’s a story that a lot of us have grown up hearing—one that says the world is boundless. That there’ll always be another field to farm, more forests to cut, more resources just waiting to be found. It’s a story that’s fueled dreams, built empires, and sent explorers across oceans.
But here’s the thing—the world isn’t endless. Every field has an edge. Every forest, a last tree. For a long time, it was easy to believe in limitless abundance. The land seemed to stretch on forever, and what we needed always felt within reach. But as cities got bigger, and technology advanced, those boundaries started showing up in ways we just couldn’t ignore.
Think about a small farming community. Back in the day, families believed the land would always provide. They’d plant the same crops, year after year, trusting the seasons. But slowly, things changed. Yields got smaller. The soil, once rich and dark, faded to something pale and thin. Some families packed up, searching for new places. Others stayed, hoping next year would be different. Most didn’t realize—they weren’t just unlucky. The land itself was worn out, exhausted after years of use.
This isn’t just a story about one community. It’s happened on a bigger scale, too. As nations grew, as industries boomed, the demands kept climbing—more fuel for factories, more water for cities, more food for more people. But the world’s ability to keep up? That didn’t grow in the same way. Soon enough, it became obvious: the idea of endless growth was just that—a comforting story.
It’s easy to fall into the habit of believing that tomorrow will always bring more. But every system—whether it’s a field, a forest, or an entire planet—has its limits. The real challenge is spotting those limits before we cross them. Can we learn to live within what we have, instead of always pushing for more?
The idea of endless growth—it’s tempting to believe. But it’s risky. It lets us ignore warning signs, put off tough choices, and hope someone else will fix things. But if history’s taught us anything, it’s that the world isn’t as forgiving as we hope. The sooner we face up to reality and accept that there are limits, the sooner we can start building a future that actually lasts.
